title: Morning inbox sort into labeled queues
summary: Each morning SI sorts the shared inbox into clear queues. It flags what is urgent. It leaves draft replies for a person to review.
problem: A shared inbox mixes customer questions, vendor mail, invoices, newsletters, and spam. Urgent messages get buried. The first hour of the day goes to figuring out what needs attention. That time should go to answering it.
what_si_does: SI reads new messages. It applies labels you define. Examples: new request, existing customer, billing, vendor, needs owner, ignore. It pulls out the key detail for each. That can be a job address, an account name, or a requested date. It marks anything time-sensitive. It writes a short summary at the top of each queue. It leaves draft replies for routine questions. Nothing goes out without a person pressing send.
setup: Connect the inbox with permission to read, label, and draft, but not send. Write down your queue names. Write what counts as urgent. Add a handful of good past replies to match your tone. Setup is often a few days. Then you spend a week or two adjusting the rules.
human_checks: A person reviews and sends every draft. SI never sends on its own.
Messages SI is unsure about go to a 'needs a human' queue. SI does not guess.
Labels and urgency rules are reviewed after the first couple of weeks. Then they are adjusted.

examples.scenario: Overnight emails are split into emergency calls, such as no heat or an active leak. New estimate requests have the address and problem pulled out. Supplier mail is in its own pile. The dispatcher starts with the emergencies.

During busy season, client emails are labeled by client and topic. Topics include a missing document, a question about a return, and payment. Anything that mentions a notice or deadline is flagged for a partner.
Tenant emails are sorted into maintenance, rent, and lease questions. Prospective-tenant inquiries go in their own queue. Maintenance messages are marked by urgency.

copy_prompt: Go through the unread messages in [inbox] from the last [24 hours]. Label each one as [list of queues]. Mark anything that mentions [urgent terms, e.g. leak, deadline, cancel] as urgent. For each message, write a one-line summary and pull out [key details, e.g. address, account, date]. Draft replies only for messages that match these examples: [paste 3-5 good past replies]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: The day starts with a sorted list instead of a raw inbox. Urgent messages are less likely to sit unseen.

title: A weekly list of emails still waiting on you
summary: Once a week SI finds threads still waiting on your reply. A customer, client, or vendor may be waiting. SI lists them with a suggested next step.
problem: Some emails get read and set aside for later. Then they never get answered. Nobody notices until the other person follows up. They are annoyed, or they take their business elsewhere.
what_si_does: SI scans received and sent mail for the past few weeks. It finds threads where the last message came from someone else. That message asked a question or requested something. It skips newsletters, notifications, and threads that were clearly closed. The result is a short list. It is grouped by who is waiting, how long they have waited, and what they asked. Simple ones get a draft reply.
setup: Read access to the mailbox. Add draft access if you want replies drafted. Give a list of senders or domains to ignore. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: A person decides which threads actually need a reply. That person sends any drafts.
Threads involving complaints or money are flagged for the owner. They are not drafted.
The ignore list is updated as false alarms show up.

examples.scenario: Friday afternoon, the principal gets a list of six client and consultant emails with open questions. One is a structural engineer waiting on a drawing revision for nine days.
The list shows two clients who asked about adding a driver to their policy. They never heard back. A carrier underwriter is waiting on a signed form.
Three inquiry emails about spring events are surfaced. Each includes the requested date and headcount. This happens before those dates get booked by someone else.

copy_prompt: Look through my inbox [mailbox] for the last [21] days. Find threads where the most recent message is from someone else and they asked a question or requested something. Ignore [newsletters, notifications, these senders]. List each one with who is waiting, how many days, and what they asked. Draft short replies for the simple ones only. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer people fall through the cracks. The weekly list makes it easier to close loops. That happens before they turn into complaints.

title: Answering where-is-it questions from your records
summary: A customer asks about an order, job, repair, or application. SI looks it up in your system. Then it drafts an accurate reply.
problem: Many incoming messages are some version of 'where is my thing?' Answering each one means opening another system. Then you find the record and write the same kind of message again.
what_si_does: SI spots status questions. It finds the matching record by name, number, address, or email. It reads the current state. That can be shipped with a tracking number. It can be a technician scheduled. It can be a part on order. It can be waiting on the customer. It drafts a reply in your tone with the real details. It flags cases where the record looks stuck. It also flags cases that contradict what the customer was told. It can also watch for a package that has not moved. The draft uses only what the record says.
setup: Give read access to the system that holds status. That can be an order system, a job tool, a repair log, or a shared sheet. Also give access to the inbox or helpdesk. Share a few example replies. Write the rules for when a delay should go to a person. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: A person approves each reply until the drafts are right most of the time. They can keep approving after that.
Anything that looks stuck or overdue goes to a person. The record is attached.
SI does not promise dates that are not in the record.
A person decides whether to contact the customer, the carrier, or wait.
SI does not promise a delivery date that is not on the scan.
Address changes and claims are made by a person.

examples.scenario: A customer emails asking about their dishwasher. SI finds the ticket. The part is on backorder with an expected date. SI drafts a reply with that date and an offer to call.
A homeowner asks when installation will happen. SI checks the production board. The doors are in finishing. SI drafts a reply with the current stage and the scheduled install week.
A 'where is my order' email is matched to the order. Tracking shows it stalled for five days. The draft apologizes and offers a replacement option. The owner still must approve it.

examples.business_type: Shopify store using a shipping app
examples.scenario: Two packages show a delivery exception and one has no scan in five days. The list and draft notes wait for the owner.
A failed delivery marked 'need new address' is listed with the order. A draft asks the customer to confirm the door code.
Weekend scans lag, so SI still lists exceptions. It flags ones that already have a customer email so you do not double-reply.

copy_prompt: For each message in [inbox/queue] asking about the status of [an order/job/repair], find the matching record in [system or file] using [order number, name, email or address]. Draft a reply that states the current status and next step using only what is in the record. Flag any record with no update in [5] days. Use this tone: [example reply]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Routine status questions get faster, more accurate answers. Stuck jobs or orders come to light sooner.
aliases: Answering 'where is it?' questions from your own records
Shipping exceptions and a 'where is my package' watch

title: Refunds, returns, and exchanges checked against your policy
summary: SI checks each refund, return, cancellation, or reschedule request against your written policy. Then it drafts the answer for approval.
problem: Requests to cancel, return, or get money back are handled differently depending on who answers. Some get approved that should not. Others get refused that should have been honored. Both lead to friction.
what_si_does: SI reads the request. It finds the relevant record. That can be the purchase date, booking date, deposit paid, or contract terms. It compares that with your written policy. It labels the request as clearly within policy, clearly outside, or a judgment call. It drafts the reply with the reason in plain language. Judgment calls go to the owner with the facts laid out. A warehouse can get the same prep list for a return. A person still approves the refund.
setup: Give SI your written policy. Give read access to the records. Point to the inbox or form where requests arrive. Setup is often a few days. Most of that time is spent turning an informal policy into clear rules.
human_checks: A person approves every refund, credit, or fee waiver. SI never issues money.
Judgment calls and upset customers go to the owner.
The policy document is the source of truth. SI does not invent exceptions.
Refunds, store credit, and exchanges are issued by a person.
Condition on arrival is confirmed by the warehouse, not guessed from a photo.
Items that might be unsafe to restock go to a person.

examples.scenario: A member asks to cancel mid-contract after moving. SI checks the membership terms. It finds the relocation clause. It drafts a reply listing the proof needed.
A couple asks to move their date. SI checks the contract's change terms and deposit rules. It drafts options for the manager to choose between.
A return request arrives 40 days after delivery. SI notes it is outside the 30-day window. The item was delivered damaged. SI marks it as a judgment call.
An exchange for size M is requested. SI notes size M is at one unit. It drafts a dock note to inspect the returned size S before restocking.
A damaged-table return is tagged quarantine per the written rules. SI does not suggest putting it back for sale.
A used personal-care return is listed as discard, with a refund draft waiting for the owner.

copy_prompt: Here is my policy for [refunds/returns/cancellations]: [paste]. For each request in [inbox/form], find the record in [system/file], and decide whether it is within policy, outside policy, or a judgment call. Draft a reply that explains the decision in plain language. List judgment calls separately with the facts. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Requests get consistent answers. The owner only sees the cases that need a real decision.
aliases: Refunds, returns and cancellations checked against your policy
Returns and exchange handling prep for the warehouse

title: FAQ and reply drafts from answers you already wrote
summary: SI reads past replies to customers. It groups the questions that keep coming up. Then it drafts a plain FAQ or help page for you to edit.
problem: The same questions arrive every week. The best answers are scattered across old emails. Different people wrote them. New staff reinvent answers. Customers cannot find them on their own.
what_si_does: SI goes through a few months of sent replies. It groups similar questions. It picks the clearest past answer for each. Then it rewrites it into a short FAQ entry. It notes where past answers disagreed so you can decide which is right. It lists questions that may deserve a policy rather than an answer. A store can turn past tickets into the same reply drafts. You still edit them.
setup: An export of a few months of replies, or read access to the helpdesk. Setup is often a few days. Then you spend editing time on your side.
human_checks: The owner approves every answer before it is published.
Conflicting past answers are resolved by a person.
Anything involving prices, guarantees, or legal terms is double-checked.
A person edits and publishes every macro.
Conflicting past answers are resolved by a person, not averaged.
Refund, discount, and legal wording is checked before a macro goes live.

examples.scenario: Past emails produce entries on vaccine schedules, what to bring to a first visit, and after-hours emergency options. The front desk reviews them.
Questions about access hours, unit sizes, insurance, and move-out notice become a single page. Staff can link to it.
Repeated client questions about support hours, change requests, and billing become an onboarding FAQ. It is sent with every new contract.
'Where is my order' and 'how do I start a return' become two macros with order and tracking fields. They come from the replies staff already send.
Shade-match threads produce three drafts. One is flagged because past answers promised a result the policy does not.
A 'will it arrive by Friday' macro is drafted to use only the carrier date already on the order.

copy_prompt: Read these past replies [export or folder]. Group the questions that come up more than [3] times. For each group, write a short FAQ entry using the clearest past answer, in plain language. List any groups where past answers disagree. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Fewer repeat questions. Faster onboarding of new staff. Answers that match from person to person.
aliases: Building an FAQ from answers you have already written
customer service macros from past tickets
Customer-service macros drafted from past tickets

title: Review requests and replies
summary: SI drafts a request for a review and a reply to a public review. You approve both before they go out.
problem: Reviews and comments arrive on several platforms. Answering them slips. Negative reviews sit unanswered for weeks. Genuine questions in comments get lost among the noise.
what_si_does: SI collects new reviews and comments. It sorts them into praise, question, complaint, and spam. It drafts short replies for the ones that need one. Complaints get a careful, non-defensive draft. That draft offers to take the talk offline. Complaints are flagged for the owner. SI never argues. SI never reveals private details. A contractor, a clinic, and a shop can use the same drafts. You still post them.
setup: Access or exports from the review and social platforms you use. Plus a few examples of replies you like. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: Every public reply is approved by a person before posting.
Complaints go straight to the owner. So does anything mentioning safety, injury, or legal threats.
Replies never include private customer details.
A staff member or clinician approves before anything goes to a patient, a payer, or any outside party.
SI never sends, submits, bills, or posts on its own.
Anything unusual goes to a "needs clinician or manager review" queue.

examples.scenario: A two-star review about a long wait gets a calm draft. It acknowledges the night, without excuses. It invites the guest to contact the manager.
Questions in social comments about insurance claims are flagged. The draft points people to call for an estimate.
Positive reviews get short thank-you drafts. Those drafts avoid confirming the reviewer is a patient.
A review-request draft goes to the whole recent-visit list, not a hand-picked happy subset. Staff approve it before it is sent.
A public reply draft thanks the reviewer and gives the practice phone number. It does not say the reviewer was a patient. It includes no before-and-after language.
Reply options for a public comment invite a phone call and mention no care. A person posts only the version they approve.

copy_prompt: Here are new reviews and comments from [platforms] since [date]: [paste or export]. Sort them into praise, question, complaint and spam. Draft a reply for each praise, question and complaint in this tone: [examples]. Keep complaints calm, short and offer to continue privately. Do not mention any personal details. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
tools_examples: Google Workspace (plans that offer a BAA)
effect: Reviews and comments get answered more often in the same way. The owner sees complaints early.
caution: Medical, dental, and other health practices should never confirm someone is a patient. Do not discuss care in a public reply. Keep replies generic. Check privacy rules that apply to you. Do not confirm that someone is a patient or a client in a public reply. A person posts every reply.
aliases: Replies to online reviews and public comments
Review requests and public reply drafts
Review requests and review-reply drafts for owner approval

title: A website or messaging chat assistant that hands hard cases to a person
summary: SI answers common questions in chat from your own website and documents. It passes anything unusual to a person. The chat is attached.
problem: People ask the same questions in chat or messaging apps at all hours. Either someone answers late. Or the chat widget is a form that just says we will get back to you.
what_si_does: SI answers from an approved set of sources. Those sources are your website, FAQ, price list, and policies. It can collect details for a quote or booking request. When a question falls outside its sources, it stops. It also stops if the question involves a complaint. It also stops if the person asks for a human. It says someone will follow up. Then it sends the chat summary to staff.
setup: An approved knowledge source. The chat or messaging tool. Clear rules for handoff. Setup is often one to two weeks. That includes testing with real questions.
human_checks: SI answers only from approved sources. It says so when it does not know.
Anything involving money, complaints, or exceptions is handed to a person.
Staff review a sample of chats each week. They correct answers.

examples.scenario: A visitor asks whether spring cleanups are still available in their town. SI confirms the service area. It collects the address and yard size. Then it sends the request to the office.
SI answers questions about office hours, consultation fees, and what documents to bring. It hands any question about a specific case to staff.
SI explains class levels and start dates. It collects placement-test requests.

copy_prompt: Using only these sources [website pages, FAQ, price list], answer customer questions in [chat/WhatsApp]. If a question is not covered, involves a complaint or money, or the person asks for a human, say that someone will follow up within [time] and send a summary to [staff contact]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Common questions get answered when the office is closed. Staff pick up the chats that need them. They have the context in hand.
caution: Law, medical, and financial offices: the assistant should share general office facts only. It should never share anything that reads as advice on a specific situation.

title: Follow-ups for quotes and estimates that went quiet
summary: SI finds quotes and estimates with no reply after a set number of days. Then it drafts a short, specific follow-up for each one.
problem: Quotes go out and then nothing happens. Following up feels awkward and gets skipped. Work is lost to whoever simply called back.
what_si_does: SI checks your quotes or estimates for ones still open after a set period. It reads what was quoted and any notes. It drafts a short follow-up that refers to the actual job. It suggests a different angle on the second follow-up. That can be a question or a scheduling option. It marks quotes to close out after the last attempt. The same follow-up fits a contractor's estimate. The owner still approves the price and sends the note.
setup: Read access to where quotes live. That can be an estimating tool, CRM, accounting system, or a folder of PDFs. Draft access to email. Your follow-up timing. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: A person approves each follow-up before it is sent.
Quotes the owner wants to handle personally are excluded.
Nothing is discounted or changed without the owner's decision.
The owner or office manager approves before anything goes to a customer, vendor, or inspector.
SI never sends a quote, takes a payment, books a job, or submits anything on its own.
Urgent or unusual items go to a "needs owner review" queue.

examples.scenario: Twelve estimates from the last month are open. Each gets a draft that mentions the roof type. It also mentions the crew's next opening in that neighborhood.
A quote for event banners has had no reply for a week. The draft asks whether the event date is still on. It notes the latest order date for delivery in time.
Prospects who received a monthly-service proposal get a follow-up. It offers a short call to walk through the scope.
Open quotes are listed with the date sent and the amount the owner entered. Follow-up drafts wait for the owner.
Quotes the owner marked for a personal call are highlighted. They do not get a standard note.
A follow-up draft uses the owner's wording. It does not change or discount the price.

copy_prompt: Here are open quotes [file/export] with date sent, customer, job and amount. For each quote older than [7] days with no reply, draft a short follow-up that mentions the specific job and offers [a next step]. For quotes already followed up [2] times, suggest closing them. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: More quotes get a timely follow-up. The pipeline reflects what is really still open.
caution: The owner approves every quote follow-up. SI does not change the price.
aliases: Follow-ups for quotes and estimates that went quiet
Quote and estimate follow-up for owner review

title: Call notes into a follow-up email and tasks
summary: After a sales or client call, SI turns your notes or the transcript into a recap email. It also makes CRM updates and dated tasks.
problem: After a call, the follow-up email and the CRM update are the first things to slip. Details are forgotten. Promised next steps happen late or not at all.
what_si_does: SI starts from typed notes, a voice memo, or a call transcript. It writes a short recap. The recap covers what the client needs and what was agreed. It covers open questions. It covers who does what by when. It drafts the follow-up email. It updates the CRM fields. It creates tasks with due dates.
setup: A way to get notes or transcripts to SI. Access to the CRM and email drafts. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: The person who was on the call reviews the recap and email before sending.
Pricing or commitments in the recap are checked against what was actually said.
Recording only happens with the consent required where you operate.

examples.scenario: A discovery call transcript becomes a recap. It lists the client's goals and the two campaigns discussed. It includes a promise to send a proposal by Thursday. A task is created for it.
A rep's voice memo from a site visit becomes notes. The notes cover roof orientation and the homeowner's financing question. A follow-up email has the requested information.
Notes from a call with a medical office about backups become a task list. An email confirms the next meeting.

copy_prompt: Here are my notes or transcript from a call with [client]: [paste]. Write a recap with needs, decisions, open questions and next steps with owners and dates. Draft a follow-up email in my voice. List the CRM fields to update and tasks to create. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Follow-ups go out while the call is fresh. The CRM reflects what was actually agreed.
caution: Call recording: consent rules differ by state and country. Some require every party to agree. Tell participants. Follow the stricter rule if you are unsure.

title: First-draft proposals from discovery notes
summary: SI turns discovery notes and your past proposals into a structured first draft. The draft has scope, timeline, and pricing options for you to edit.
problem: Proposals take hours to write. They often start from a copy of an old one. Leftover details from another client remain. The delay means the prospect waits while interest cools.
what_si_does: SI reads the discovery notes and a few of your past proposals. Then it drafts a proposal in your usual structure. It states the client's situation in their words. It covers scope and what is not included. It covers timeline. It covers pricing options from your rate sheet. It covers next steps. It highlights any section where it lacked information. It does not guess.
setup: Your proposal template. A rate sheet. Two or three good past proposals. Setup is often a day or two.
human_checks: The owner reviews scope and pricing line by line.
SI does not invent pricing. It uses the rate sheet and flags gaps.
Nothing is sent to the prospect without approval.

examples.scenario: Notes from a walkthrough become a proposal. It covers demolition, plumbing, and tile scope. It includes an allowance line for fixtures. It flags that cabinet sizes are still unknown.
A discovery call becomes a proposal with three package options. The timeline is built from the studio's standard phases.
Notes from a meeting with a 40-person company become a proposal outline. It includes the review steps. One section is marked for the consultant to fill in.

copy_prompt: Using these discovery notes [paste], my template [file], rate sheet [file] and these past proposals [files], draft a proposal for [client]. Include situation, scope, exclusions, timeline, [2-3] pricing options and next steps. Mark any section where information is missing. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Proposals go out sooner. They start from a clean, client-specific draft instead of a recycled one.

title: A one-page brief on a prospect before you meet
summary: Before a meeting or pitch, SI gathers public facts about the prospect. It also gathers your past contact. Then it writes a short brief.
problem: Walking into a meeting unprepared costs credibility. Researching every prospect takes time nobody has. Past emails and notes about the account are scattered.
what_si_does: SI reads the prospect's website, recent public news, and any public profiles you point it to. It also reads your own CRM notes and past emails. It produces a one-page brief. The brief covers what they do. It covers size and locations if public. It covers recent changes. It covers who you are meeting. It covers past contact. It lists three questions worth asking. Sources are listed so you can check them.
setup: Read access to your CRM and email. A list of sources you consider acceptable. Setup is often a day.
human_checks: The person meeting the prospect checks facts against the listed sources.
SI uses public and your own information only.
Anything uncertain is marked as such. It is not stated as fact.

examples.scenario: Before meeting a growing restaurant group, the brief notes the two new locations opening. It notes the current carrier mentioned in an old email. It lists questions about liquor liability.
A brief on a regional manufacturer covers its open job postings. It covers recent plant expansion news. It covers the last talk with its HR manager.
Before a school district interview, the brief summarizes the district's published facilities plan. It also covers past projects of similar size.

copy_prompt: Prepare a one-page brief on [organization] for a meeting on [date] with [names]. Use their website [URL], these public sources [list], and my CRM notes and emails about them. Include what they do, recent changes, who I am meeting, past contact with us, and [3] good questions. List sources for every fact. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Meetings start better prepared. There is less last-minute scrambling.

title: Personal outreach drafts and reply handling you approve
summary: SI drafts first-touch and follow-up messages from real research. It sorts the replies. It offers meeting times. You approve every message.
problem: Generic outreach gets ignored. Personal outreach takes too long to write. Replies, when they come, sit unsorted. Interested people go cold.
what_si_does: SI starts from a list of prospects and a short brief on each. It drafts a short first message that refers to something specific and relevant. It also drafts one or two follow-ups. When replies come in, it sorts them. Groups are interested, not now, wrong person, and no. It drafts an answer for each. For the interested ones, it proposes open times from your calendar. Unsubscribe and no-contact requests are recorded and respected.
setup: Your prospect list. Calendar access. A clear description of what you offer. Setup is often several days.
human_checks: Every message is approved before sending. Volume stays modest.
Opt-outs are honored immediately and recorded.
Outreach follows the anti-spam and privacy rules that apply to you.

examples.scenario: Drafts to office managers at nearby firms mention their recent move into a new building. They offer a tasting. Replies asking for menus get a draft with the menu and two tasting times.
Property managers of older buildings get a note about seasonal maintenance. A 'not now, try in spring' reply becomes a dated reminder.
Small nonprofits with an upcoming grant cycle get a short note. It offers a review of last year's application.

copy_prompt: For each prospect in [list] with these notes [research], draft a first message of under [100] words that mentions one specific, relevant detail and offers [offer]. Draft [2] short follow-ups. Then sort these replies [paste] into interested, not now, wrong person and no, and draft an answer for each, offering times from [calendar]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Outreach becomes more personal without taking all afternoon. Interested replies get answered quickly.
caution: Outbound email and messaging are regulated. One example is CAN-SPAM in the US. Rules in the EU and Canada are stricter. Include opt-out handling. Follow the rules that apply to you.

title: Check-ins for customers who are due
summary: SI spots regular customers who are past their usual reorder or rebooking interval. Then it drafts a friendly, specific check-in.
problem: Repeat customers are the easiest business to keep. Nobody tracks when each one is due. They drift away quietly. Or they simply buy from whoever reached out first.
what_si_does: SI reads your order, invoice, or appointment history. It works out each regular customer's usual interval. It lists those who are overdue. For each, it drafts a short check-in. The check-in mentions what they usually order or book. It offers an easy next step. A seasonal shop can use the same draft when the season opens. A person sends it.
setup: An export of order, invoice, or booking history. Draft access to email or text. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: A person reviews the list and approves each message.
Customers who asked not to be contacted are excluded.
Customers with open complaints or unpaid balances are flagged instead of nudged.
A person reviews the list and approves each message or the batch wording.
A person approves anything that sends, pays, orders, or posts.
People who asked not to be contacted are excluded before anything is sent.

examples.scenario: A cafe that orders every two weeks has not ordered in four. The draft mentions their usual blend. It asks whether anything changed.
Customers who booked an opening last spring but not this spring get a reminder. Open dates are included.
Clients who usually book every six weeks and are now at nine get a text draft. It offers their stylist's next openings.
Last spring's opening list gets a draft that names the weeks you are actually booking. It asks them to reply with a preferred week, with no promise that a date is free.
Last summer's email list gets a draft with opening weekend hours you typed in. Anyone who unsubscribed is left off.
Last December's buyers get a draft that the shop is open again on the dates you named. It includes the gift-wrap hours you supplied and no invented sale.

copy_prompt: Using this order or booking history [file], find each customer's usual interval between [orders/visits]. List customers who are more than [50%] past their usual interval, with their last date and usual purchase. Draft a short check-in for each in this tone: [example]. Exclude [do-not-contact list]. Pause and show me before sending, submitting, posting or changing anything.
effect: Regular customers hear from you before they drift. The outreach feels personal rather than mass-mailed.
aliases: Check-ins for repeat customers who are due

title: Supplier invoices into draft bills
summary: SI reads supplier invoices from email. It drafts the bill, flags a duplicate, and notes the tax. You approve it before it is saved.
problem: Invoices arrive as PDFs in several inboxes. Someone retypes them into the accounting system. Duplicates, typos, and missed due dates follow.
what_si_does: SI watches an invoices inbox. It reads each attachment. It extracts supplier, invoice number, date, due date, line totals, and tax. It creates a draft bill with a suggested account based on past coding. It checks for problems. Those include an invoice number already entered. They include an amount that does not match the purchase order. They include missing tax registration details. They include a changed bank account on the invoice. It can also bundle the month's vendor invoices for your accountant. A separate job still checks for a supplier price increase. You approve every bill.
setup: A dedicated invoices inbox or forwarding rule. Accounting access limited to creating drafts. Your past coding as a reference. Setup is often a few days.
human_checks: The bookkeeper reviews and approves each draft bill.
SI never pays bills. SI never changes supplier bank details.
A change in a supplier's payment details is always flagged. It is confirmed by phone with a known contact.
A person confirms a flag before anyone pays or voids a bill.
SI does not pay, code, or file tax on its own.
Odd matches stay on a review list and are not forced to match.

examples.scenario: Lumber and electrical supply invoices are turned into draft bills tagged to the right job. A second copy of the same invoice sent by a supplier's rep is caught.
Weekly produce, meat, and linen invoices become draft bills. Food and non-food costs are coded separately.
Vendor invoices for repairs are matched to the property and unit. One arriving with new bank details is flagged before anyone pays it.
A parts bill matches last week's invoice number, and it is flagged before payables run.
A vendor bill has no tax on a taxable line, and the draft note waits for the bookkeeper.
Two PDFs from the same supplier show the same total and date, and one is marked as a likely duplicate.

Opt-in and unsubscribe rules are followed.

human_checks: The hiring manager approves the posting before it is published.
Requirements are checked to be job-related.
A person confirms pay transparency and posting rules where you hire.

Criteria and outcomes are reviewed from time to time so they stay the same and fair.

title: A first read of contracts for the terms that matter
